source.title: Memorization Without Overfitting: Analyzing the Training Dynamics of Large Language Models
source.authors: Kushal Tirumala; Aram H. Markosyan; Luke Zettlemoyer; Armen Aghajanyan

record.file_problem: none; full paper text, including appendix, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures exact training-context memorization and forgetting during language-model training, but does not measure the natural-label test error or training–test generalization gap described by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The reported outcomes concern memorization on training data or on a validation special batch after it is deliberately introduced into training. They do not test whether models that fit random labels generalize on natural labels, the listed image-classifier comparisons, or the other version-specific claims. Results cited from prior work are not extracted.
record.test_reason: The study measures training-token prediction accuracy and retention after deliberate exposure, not any version's specified generalization comparison. R4 measures memorization before validation perplexity first increases, but does not compare random and natural labels (V1) or test error beyond an interpolation threshold (V2). Its memorization metric also differs from V8's inclusion-based influence measure, and no example-removal experiment is performed.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that larger language models generally memorize faster and have higher post-exposure forgetting baselines, and advocate measuring memorization alongside cross-entropy. Their detailed results qualify the speed claim for early, low-threshold masked language modeling on WIKITEXT-103.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses causal and masked language modeling on text corpora and defines exact token-context memorization as argmax accuracy. It does not reproduce the original studies or test the listed image-classification generalization claims.
record.method_sensitivity: Memorization dynamics vary with model size, language-modeling task, threshold, dataset size, learning rate, unique identifiers, part of speech, special-batch injection frequency, and repetition spacing.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger models generally reach high training-token accuracy faster. On WIKITEXT-103 masked language modeling, smaller models reach low thresholds faster initially.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Language-model training memorization speed depends on scale, task, dataset, and accuracy threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger models memorize more before validation perplexity first increases. Separately, their faster memorization persists at fixed learning rates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Greater training memorization can precede validation-perplexity deterioration, and scale-dependent memorization speed is not explained solely by learning-rate differences.

fits_no_version.finding: Expanding the dictionary accelerates memorization, and using the added tokens as unique identifiers produces an additional gain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dictionary expansion and explicit example identifiers can accelerate training-token memorization.

fits_no_version.finding: Nouns, proper nouns, and numerals are learned faster than verbs and adjectives; contiguous memorized sequences lengthen during training, faster in the larger model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-token memorization varies by linguistic category and develops into longer contiguous sequences over training.

fits_no_version.finding: After special-batch exposure, accuracy approaches a baseline that rises with model scale and repeated exposure. Spacing and injection checkpoint have minimal effects; perplexity can keep rising after accuracy flattens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-exposure token retention during continued language-model training depends on scale and exposure count, and accuracy can reveal behavior obscured by perplexity.

record.problems: The paper notes that its exact-memorization definition ignores model confidence and does not normalize for training-set duplication. Most plotted outcomes have no exact numerical values in the supplied text; the reported findings are primarily qualitative. The special batch is deliberately introduced into training, so these forgetting results do not measure ordinary held-out generalization.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible results omitted. Values shown only in figures are recorded qualitatively where the text explicitly describes their trends; no exact values were inferred from plots.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the comparison of held-out accuracy under natural versus random labels.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier generalization, including local connectivity and initialization effects.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD on held-out performance under specified tuning conditions.
Large versus small batches on held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout effects on held-out error. Setting dropout to zero throughout provides no dropout comparison.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with other measures.
Identifying memorized examples through inclusion-based influence, removing them, retraining, and comparing test accuracy with random removal.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8, because none measures a version's specified effect; this does not reject the reported memorization trends. No omitted result in the supplied text warrants a version-specific verdict. The paper cites original generalization work but supplies no direct test of these versions.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fit random labels or compare held-out accuracy on natural labels with held-out accuracy on random labels.
Does not sweep one-hidden-layer ReLU width against interpolation or test error.
Does not compare convolutional and fully connected image classifiers.
Does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD on held-out performance.
Does not compare large and small batches on held-out performance.
Does not test dropout effects on held-out error.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare it with generalization gaps.
Does not identify and remove memorized examples, then measure test accuracy.

rows.subject: 125M, 355M, 1.3B, 2.7B, 6.7B, and 13B model configurations
rows.operation_detail: Measured epochs per training example needed to reach exact training-context memorization thresholds as model size varied.
rows.measure: T(N, τ), number of times each training example must be seen to reach the threshold of memorized training contexts.
rows.value: Larger models generally memorize faster; for τ = 0.9, T(N, 0.9) is monotonically decreasing in N. For τ from 0.4 to 0.95, T(N, τ) is generally decreasing with N.
rows.note: Trend and monotonicity are described in the text; precise plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: The reported memorization-speed trend is supported, but training-token accuracy does not measure any version's effect.

rows.subject: 125M, 355M, 1.3B, 2.7B, 6.7B, and 13B model configurations
rows.operation_detail: Measured epochs per training example needed to reach exact training-context memorization thresholds as model size varied.
rows.measure: T(N, τ), number of times each training example must be seen to reach the threshold of memorized training contexts.
rows.value: T(N, τ) is not monotonically decreasing in N for lower τ values and is monotonically decreasing for higher τ values; the transition occurs between τ = 0.6 and τ = 0.7. Smaller models memorize faster initially and slower in the long run.
rows.note: The text describes the trends and transition; precise plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: The threshold-dependent reversal in memorization speed is supported; it is not partial evidence for any claim version.

rows.subject: 125M, 355M, 1.3B, 2.7B, 6.7B, and 13B model configurations
rows.operation_detail: Measured gradient updates needed to reach exact memorization thresholds on the batch presented at each update.
rows.measure: Tupdate(N, τ), updates needed to reach the threshold on the batch given at that update.
rows.value: Tupdate(N, τ) is monotonically decreasing with N for the plotted thresholds.
rows.note: The text describes the trend; precise plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: The causal-language-modeling result is supported but measures training-batch accuracy. Figure 3 also reports the same scale trend for masked language modeling, which this row does not capture.

rows.subject: 125M, 355M, 1.3B, 2.7B, 6.7B, and 13B model configurations
rows.operation_detail: Measured the proportion of training data memorized before validation perplexity first increased, as model size varied.
rows.measure: M(f) before overfitting, where overfitting is defined as the first epoch when validation perplexity increases.
rows.value: Larger models generally memorize more before overfitting.
rows.note: The text describes the trend; precise plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: Correctly reports more memorization before the first validation-perplexity increase. Neither random-label generalization nor test error beyond a width interpolation threshold is measured.

rows.subject: 125M, 355M, 1.3B, 2.7B, and 6.7B model configurations
rows.operation_detail: Measured training-context memorization speed across a range of learning rates.

conditions.value: standard range; exact values appear only in figure

rows.measure: T(N, 0.9), epochs per training example needed to reach 0.9 exact memorization.
rows.value: At a fixed learning rate, larger models reach 0.9 memorization faster. T(N, 0.9) initially falls and then rises as learning rate increases; sensitivity to learning rate generally decreases with model size.
rows.note: The text describes the trends; exact learning-rate values and plotted measurements are not transcribed.
rows.check: The learning-rate comparisons concern training memorization speed, not held-out performance or an optimizer comparison.

rows.subject: 125M model with increased dictionary size but without using the added tokens
rows.size_stated: 125M model; added dictionary tokens increase model size
rows.operation_detail: Added unused tokens to the dictionary to control for the size increase from adding unique identifiers.
rows.measure: Exact training-context memorization M(f) over epochs.
rows.value: Increasing dictionary size alone improves the speed of memorization.
rows.note: The text describes the comparison; precise plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: The dictionary-expansion control is correctly described, but its outcome is training memorization speed.

rows.subject: 125M model with unique identifiers
rows.size_stated: 125M model; dictionary expansion adds output parameters
rows.operation_detail: Prepended a unique integer document ID to every training example and measured memorization over epochs.
rows.measure: Exact training-context memorization M(f) over epochs.
rows.baseline: Original 125M model and the increased-dictionary-size control
rows.value: Using the unique identifiers yields an additional gain in memorization speed; prompting with a document ID shifts the dynamics away from being monotonically increasing over time.
rows.note: The text describes the comparisons; precise plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: The identifier intervention accelerates training memorization; no version's generalization outcome is measured.

rows.subject: 355M model
rows.operation_detail: Tracked correctly predicted parts of speech and exactly memorized tokens by part of speech over training.

conditions.value: numerals, proper nouns, nouns, verbs, adjectives

rows.measure: R(p), proportion with the correct part of speech; and Rmem(p), proportion of exactly memorized tokens for part of speech p.
rows.value: Nouns, proper nouns, and numerals are memorized noticeably faster than verbs and adjectives for both R(p) and Rmem(p); all considered parts of speech are eventually memorized.
rows.note: The text states the comparative trends; precise plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: The part-of-speech trends are supported. R(p) measures correct token category rather than exact token prediction; neither measure tests a claim version.

rows.subject: 2.7B model
rows.operation_detail: Measured exact memorization on a validation special batch after one introduction, while standard training continued on the training set.
rows.measure: Exact memorization M(f) on the special batch over continued training.
rows.value: Special-batch memorization degrades quickly at first and then slows exponentially, approaching a forgetting baseline.
rows.note: The text describes the curve; precise plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: The forgetting trend is supported, but the special batch has been trained on and therefore does not measure held-out generalization.

rows.subject: 125M, 355M, 1.3B, 2.7B, 6.7B, and 13B model configurations
rows.operation_detail: Compared the minimum observed special-batch memorization during training across model sizes.
rows.measure: Forgetting baseline, approximated by the lowest special-batch memorization throughout training.
rows.value: The forgetting baseline increases monotonically with model scale.
rows.note: The text states monotonic increase; precise plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: The scale-dependent retention trend is supported. There is no pre-exposure baseline establishing how much retained accuracy was caused by the special-batch exposure, and no claim version is tested.

rows.subject: 125M model
rows.operation_detail: Repeatedly injected the validation special batch before continuing training on the training set alone.
rows.value: The forgetting baseline increases monotonically with repetition frequency; differences in baseline value are on the order of 10⁻².
rows.note: The text describes the relationship and gives the order of the differences; exact per-condition values are not stated.
rows.check: Repeated exposure changes subsequent special-batch retention, not any version's held-out generalization outcome.

rows.subject: 125M model
rows.operation_detail: Periodically injected the validation special batch, trained on it once, and continued training on the training set alone.

conditions.value: spaced repetitions; spacing conditions shown in figure

rows.value: Spaced repetition has minimal effect on the forgetting baseline, on the order of 10⁻³, independent of spacing length.
rows.note: The authors describe the effect as minimal; exact plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: The authors describe the spacing effect as minimal, supporting absence for that separate retention comparison; this does not establish absence of any claim version's effect.

rows.subject: 125M model
rows.operation_detail: Introduced the validation special batch at different training checkpoints and measured subsequent memorization.
rows.value: The baseline is not sensitive to data batch order; maximum difference between baseline values is on the order of 10⁻³.
rows.note: The authors describe the order effect as absent at the stated scale; exact per-condition values are not stated.
rows.check: The negligible difference concerns special-batch injection at three training checkpoints, rather than general batch-order invariance or any claim version.

rows.subject: 1.3B model
rows.operation_detail: Measured special-batch exact memorization and perplexity during continued training after the batch was introduced once.
rows.measure: Special-batch M(f) and perplexity over epochs.
rows.value: Special-batch memorization flattens while perplexity continues increasing.
rows.note: The text describes both trends; precise plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: The divergence between accuracy and perplexity is supported, but both are evaluated on the deliberately trained-on special batch.

rows.subject: 2.7B and 125M models
rows.operation_detail: Tracked average length of contiguous exactly memorized token sequences during training.
rows.measure: Average memory unit length L across the training dataset.
rows.value: Average memory unit length increases over time; it increases faster for the 2.7B model than for the 125M model.
rows.note: The text describes the trend; precise plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: The contiguous-memory-length trend is supported but does not measure a claim version's generalization effect.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
